questions.question:
The number of points of intersection of \(|z-(4+3 i)|=2\) and \(|z|+|z-4|=6, z \in C\), is

 

[JEE Main 2022, 27 June (Shift 2)]
questions.explanation:
Let

\(z=x+iy\).

The equation

\(|z|+|z-4|=6\)

means

\(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}+\sqrt{(x-4)^2+y^2}=6\).

This is an ellipse whose foci are \((0,0)\) and \((4,0)\).

Its centre is the midpoint of the foci:

\((2,0)\).

Also,

\(2a=6\),

so

\(a=3\).

The distance of each focus from the centre is

\(c=2\).

Therefore,

\(b^2=a^2-c^2=9-4=5\).

Hence, the ellipse is

\(\dfrac{(x-2)^2}{9}+\dfrac{y^2}{5}=1\).

The other equation is

\(|z-(4+3i)|=2\),

so it is the circle

\((x-4)^2+(y-3)^2=4\).

The ellipse satisfies

\(-\sqrt5\leq y\leq\sqrt5\),

and

\(\sqrt5<3\).

Therefore, an intersection point with the circle must lie on the lower half of the circle.

For the upper half of the ellipse,

\(y_E=\dfrac{\sqrt5}{3}\sqrt{9-(x-2)^2}\).

For the lower half of the circle,

\(y_C=3-\sqrt{4-(x-4)^2}\).

At \(x=2\),

\(y_E=\sqrt5\)

and

\(y_C=3\),

so

\(y_E-y_C<0\).

At \(x=4\),

\(y_E=\dfrac53\)

and

\(y_C=1\),

so

\(y_E-y_C>0\).

Therefore, there is at least one intersection for

\(2<x<4\).

At \(x=5\),

\(y_E=0\)

and

\(y_C=3-\sqrt3>0\),

so

\(y_E-y_C<0\).

Therefore, there is at least one more intersection for

\(4<x<5\).

Now,

\(y_E''=-\dfrac{3\sqrt5}{\left(9-(x-2)^2\right)^{3/2}}<0\)

and

\(y_C''=\dfrac4{\left(4-(x-4)^2\right)^{3/2}}>0\).

Hence,

\((y_E-y_C)''<0\),

so \(y_E-y_C\) bends downward throughout the common interval.

A function that bends downward throughout cannot cross the \(x\)-axis more than twice when its sign changes in the order negative, positive, negative.

Thus, the two curves have exactly two points of intersection.

Therefore, the correct option is C.

Let \( \int_{\cos x}^{1} t^2f(t)dt=\sin^3x+\cos x \).

Differentiating both sides with respect to \(x\), we get

\( \sin x\cos^2x f(\cos x)=3\sin^2x\cos x-\sin x \).

So \( f(\cos x)=\frac{3\sin^2x\cos x-\sin x}{\sin x\cos^2x}=3\tan x-\sec^2x \).

Let \(y=\cos x\), then \( \sin x=\sqrt{1-y^2} \), \( \tan x=\frac{\sqrt{1-y^2}}{y} \), and \( \sec^2x=\frac{1}{y^2} \).

Thus \( f(y)=\frac{3\sqrt{1-y^2}}{y}-\frac{1}{y^2} \).

Now \( f'(y)=3\left(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-y^2}}-\frac{\sqrt{1-y^2}}{y^2}\right)+\frac{2}{y^3} \).

At \(y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), \( \sqrt{1-y^2}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \).

Therefore \( f'\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=3\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}-\sqrt{6}\right)+6\sqrt{3} \).

So \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}f'\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=3\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\sqrt{2}\right)+6 \).

Hence \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}f'\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=6-\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}-3\sqrt{2}=6-\frac{9}{\sqrt{2}} \).

Hence \(\alpha+\gamma=3\sqrt2+2\sqrt3\).

\(\alpha-\beta=2\sqrt3\).

Thus \(\alpha=\beta+2\sqrt3\).

Using \(\alpha\beta=5\),

\(\beta(\beta+2\sqrt3)=5\).

Therefore, \(\beta^2+2\sqrt3\beta-5=0\).

Solving, \(\beta=-\sqrt3\pm2\sqrt2\).

If \(\beta=-\sqrt3+2\sqrt2\),

then \(\alpha=\sqrt3+2\sqrt2\).

Thus \(\alpha+\beta=4\sqrt2\),

so \(\lambda=\sqrt2\).

Also, \(\gamma=3\sqrt2-\beta=\sqrt2+\sqrt3\).

Then \(\alpha\gamma=(\sqrt3+2\sqrt2)(\sqrt2+\sqrt3)\)

\(=7+3\sqrt6\)

Hence \(\alpha+2\beta+\gamma=4\lambda+3\sqrt2\)

\(=4\sqrt2+3\sqrt2=7\sqrt2\).
